articles.headline: Aid Fund Sought By 'Concern'
articles.body:

According to Bettina Valenta, chairman of the committee which is organizing "Concern," "Every organization on campus either has, or will receive a letter from our committee asking that they discuss the campaign and vote on a resolution supporting it."

Fraternities and sororities discussed it Monday night; Interfraternity Council, Panhellenic Council, YMCA, Circle K and the Association of Women Students are to discuss it today, and it is to be presented to Student Forum tomorrow, Miss Valenta added.

Miss Valenta stated further, "A fact sheet fully explaining the campaign and answering questions concerning it will be distributed to the students within the next two days."

The sheet states that 1) Any funds raised will be added to those obtained by the University and faculty. . (and) will be used only to supplement the support the student himself can provide.

2) If, for any of numerous reasons, no students are available to come to Wesleyan, the funds raised will be contributed to the National Student Christian Federation Legal and Defense Fund to be used by them to provide legal assistance to affected students.

3) Any scholarship provided by the University will not come from the normal scholarship funds provided for Ohio Wesleyan students.

4) Before any student is accepted, he must meet the criterion for admittance established by the Admission Committee.

5) Any student who is accepted will be fully informed, prior to his coming, of minority group problems at Ohio Wesleyan and Delaware.

Miss Valenta concluded, "This is the student body's opportunity to act directly and positively in facing a problem of nationwide significance. How we react cannot help but receive widespread attention and reflect upon the University and particularly the students."

A campus-wide student campaign, called "Concern," will run May 11-13 to raise scholarship funds for Southern students who have been expelled or suspended from their colleges and universities for taking part in sit-ins or picketing demonstrations, Dick Neely, publicity chairman for the campaign, said.

Student Council President George Conrads will kick off the campaign at 1:45 p.m. May 11, and it will continue until noon, May 13, Neely added.

A collection booth will be set up on the main campus, Neely said, but he didn't specify exactly where.

The campaign, with a goal of $2,000, will be run in support of the faculty resolution providing scholarship aid for deserving Southern students, Neely added.

Although the fund-raising campaign was originated by a committee of interested students it has received the unanimous approval of Student Council, Conrads reported.

articles.headline: Monnett Week End Attractions Include Senior Show, Dolphins
articles.body:
The senior show, the Dolphin show, the Monnett style show, dormitory banquets, an ROTC parade and a convocation address by Lillian Gilbreth will highlight this year's Monnett Week End activities.

Tickets for the Friday and Saturday night performances of the Senior show, "South Pacific," have been sold out for more than a week, according to Senior Class President Jon Hillegas.

Approximately 150 reserved seat tickets for tomorrow night's performance will go on sale at the door 45 minutes before the 8:15 p.m. curtain time.

Due to the dorm banquets, Hillegas explained, the Friday performance will not begin until 8:45 p.m. The other two nights the play will begin at 8:15 p.m. in the Willis High School Auditorium.

Swim Show
The combined swimming talents of the Dolphin Club and the varsity swimming team will open their Monnett Week end presentation "The Greatest Splash on Earth" in Pfeiffer Natatorium tomorrow evening.

The water show, directed by Martha Patterson, associate professor of physical education, will present one performance Thursday and Friday evenings and two on Saturday night.

Prof. Patterson said that this year's exhibition of synchronized swimming will include a solo routine by Nancy McKain which brought her third class honors at the International Aquatic Arts Festival held in Florida, Apr. 9.

The performances will begin at 7:45 p.m. tomorrow, 9:15 p.m. Friday and 7:45 and 9:15 p.m. Saturday. Tickets are 75 cents for adults and 50 cents for children.

Dorm Banquets
The Monnett Week End banquets will be held Friday in Monnett, Stuyvesant and Austin halls, with the doors opening at 5:45 p.m.

The dorm presidents will act as hostesses. They are Bonnie Butler, Stuyvesant; Janet Klein, Monnett, and Wilhelmina Good, Austin.

Speakers include Cathy Battaglia, Stuyvesant; Margie Wagner, Monnett, and Amelia Armstrong, Austin.

Decorations of flowers and candles will be in keeping with the theme, "Prisms." Harriet

Halteman is committee chairman for the event.

Style Show

The annual Monnett Day style show, featuring outfits made in the clothing courses of the Home Economics Department will be presented for mothers Saturday at 2:30 p.m. in Gray Chapel.

"Dimensions in Design" will be the theme of the show, narrated by Nancy Judson and George Robinson. A setting of lavender, aqua, white and black colors will serve as a background for the 50 girls, who will model outfits ranging from school clothes to formal dresses in a vast assortment of colors and prints.

Immediately after the style show, a tea will be held in Sturges Hall.

Convocation

Lillian Gilbreth, noted scientist and humanitarian, will speak at the Monnett Week End Convocation service in Gray Chapel at 10:30 a.m. Sunday.

Welcoming Mrs. Gilbreth will be President David A. Lockmiller, Director of Religious Activities Richard R. Gay and Convocation Committee Chairman Linda Yannetta.

A discussion with Mrs. Gilbreth will be held in University Hall immediately following the services.

Mrs. Gilbreth is known internationally as the mother in the novel "Cheaper by the Dozen," written by two of her children.

articles.headline: 1st Semester Issues Win High Praise
articles.body:
Judge Lauds News Coverage, Editorials

Last semester's Transcript won the top national rating of All-American, the Associated Collegiate Press announced in Minneapolis, Minn., Monday. Only 43 of the 401 competing senior college newspapers received the top honor.

Entries are judged in 12 different classifications, ranging from monthlies in schools under 500 enrollment to dailies. The Transcript was entered in the fourth toughest classification — weeklies in schools from 2,001-4,000 enrollment.

Prof. Verne Edwards, Transcript adviser, said that the Transcript would probably represent the smallest of the 35 schools in that category, thus adding to the Transcript's honor.

"Among 20 Best"
Prof. Edwards said that the 118 newspapers entered in the top four classifications "would certainly represent the best newspapers put out by American colleges." This means, he said, that the Transcript is ranked as "one of the 20 best" college newspapers among the hundreds published.

Bill Darrow was editor and Sue McCabe managing editor of the first Transcript to win All-American honors in three years. In its nine past semester ratings, the Transcript has won 

TRANSCRIPT WINS MORE HONORS
The Transcript and individual members of its staff also received honors at the Ohio College Newspaper Association Convention, Saturday.

The Transcript was judged the second best weekly paper in Class I (schools with an enrollment of at least 1,500).

Tony Hirsch's picture, "Digging for Pennies," was judged the second best news photo in all Ohio College papers. "The OWU Faculty Machine," a cartoon by Max Neufeldt, earned a third place award in the OCNA competition, and Ronnie Ruch's news story, "59 Grad Recovering From Injury," was acclaimed as the third best news story in all Ohio college papers.

No Low Scores

Entries are rated from "poor" to "superior" on a seven-point scale in 23 categories. The Transcript was scored "excellent" 11 times, between "excellent" and "very good" 7 times, "very good" 4 times and "good" once. None of its scores fell in the lower three ratings.

The judges comments were most favorable on breadth, balance and "treatment" of news stories. "Few college or professional papers do as fine a job," he said in praising the Transcript's development of news value.

articles.headline: Integration Leaders Express Sit-In Views
articles.body:
Bernard Lee, a Negro student recently expelled from Alabama State University for his participation in the Southern sit-in demonstrations, and the Rev. Mr. Julius C. Herron, Program Associate for the American Baptist Home Mission Society, presented their views on Southern integration at a 4 p.m. meeting in the MUB, Monday.

The discussion, attended by about 200 students, faculty members and townspeople, consisted of talks by both Herron and Lee, followed by questions from the audience.

During the program Lee stated concerning the sit-ins, "We know the non-violent movement can work, and I ask that the students carry on 

Be sure to read the account of Associate Editor Tom Grissom's interview with Bernard Lee, page eight.

the philosophy of non-violence or none at all."

Problem Deep

He added, "The present problem in the South is greater than we realize and is far deeper than black versus white. The problem is to make certain that democratic principles are preserved at all costs."

John Priest, assistant professor of religion, observed during the discussion, "The sit-in demonstrations in the South are a civil disobedience. This constitutes an organized and deliberate infringement on the municipal or state laws there."

He added, "These laws are broken because they are thought not to be commensary with the laws of the federal government."

articles.headline: ODK Taps Seven; Dunbar President
articles.body:
Frank Dunbar was chosen Sunday from among the six new members to be next year's president of Omicron Delta Kappa, men's leadership honorary society, for the coming year.

Dennis Appleyard was elected secretary by the honorary society, and Max Urick was picked to be treasurer.

The other three juniors tapped at Friday's ODK Chapel are Al Alexander, Jon Denney and Bob Maxwell. Dean of Men Ronald Stead was also tapped.

Al Alexander, Chi Phi from East Cleveland, O., is executive vice-president of IFC.

Dennie Appleyard, Delta Tau Delta from South Haven, Mich., is editor of the Bijou and vice-president of his fraternity.

Jon Denney, Phi Kappa Psi from Lincoln, Neb., is president of IFC and his fraternity.

Frank Dunbar, Phi Delta Theta from Upper Arlington, O., is president of his fraternity and past Student Forum representative-at-large.

Bob Maxwell, Phi Delta Theta from Delaware, is presently serving as chief justice of Men's Court and president of Circle K International.

Max Urick, Sigma Chi from Troy, O., has been elected co-captain of the 1960-61 football team and is now president of the W-Clan.

Required for ODK membership is major accomplishment in athletics, debate, dramatics, journalism, music or organizational activities. A minor in another of these fields and good scholarship are also criteria for membership.

articles.headline: Confusion Delays Dress Policy Change
articles.body:
The long-disputed question of how Ohio Wesleyan coeds will dress on East Campus still remains unanswered, according to latest information from the Association of Women Students.

Confusion centering around the possible revision of the regulation will result in the return to the Administration of that group's reply to an AWS request that women's dress be left to the discretion of the individual women (see Transcript, Apr. 20).

AWS Board's misinterpretation of this reply resulted in some of the confusion, as AWS members were called upon two weeks ago to vote on this issue. The alternatives, as the Board interpreted them, were to leave the policy as is, to re-state the demand for individual discretion or to suggest specific rules governing women's dress for specific areas of campus life, Gwen Greenfield, AWS judicial president, told the Transcript last week.

If a finely delineated policy were established, thought Board members, it would be subject to Administration approval or disapproval and would take effect next fall. The Board did not feel that it could formulate any such policy without a vote of the entire membership of AWS.

Voting, however, was light (some corridors failed to hold meetings on the night designated), and results of the poll were inconclusive. Announced plans for a vote last week were changed Wednesday when AWS learned that the Administration had not meant to imply a denial of the discretion proposal or that AWS define specific restrictions. The administrative policy was explained as an attempt to determine what restrictions the women would deem appropriate should the discretion proposal prove unsatisfactory to the Administration.

Present and past judical and executive presidents of AWS, Miss Greenfield, Jan Dunham, Sue Harris and Jan Stillinger, will go personally to the Administration to clarify the latter's position and to determine what measures can be taken to change the policy.

articles.headline: Book Fund Falls Short
articles.body:
A total of $372.31 was collected from OWU students for the Freedom House Bookshelf Committee to buy American books to be sent to uncommitted countries, Lane McGaughy, representative-at-large, reported.

The goal for the campaign had been set at $1,000.

The money will enable the Freedom House Bookshelf Committee, headed by poet Archibald MacLeish, to purchase and send 46 sets of books which cost $8 per set.

The sororities contributed $247.52; fraternities, $62.64; faculty, $41 and independents $21.15.

The biggest contributors were Pi Beta Phi, $82; Alpha Gamma Delta, $40; Chi Omega, $27; Alpha Tau Omega, $27; Zeta Tau Alpha, $25, and Independent Men's Club, $18. All of the sororities and independent women contributed.

The fraternities who contributed, besides Alpha Tau Omega, were Beta Theta Pi, Beta Sigma Tau, Sigma Alpha Epsilon, Sigma Phi Epsilon and Tau Kappa Epsilon.

McGaughy said that all of the fraternity reps agreed to support the campaign and that each fraternity president was contacted.

The eight fraternities which did not contribute were Alpha Sigma Phi, Chi Phi, Kappa Sigma, Delta Tau Delta, Phi Delta Theta, Phi Gamma Delta, Phi Kappa Psi and Sigma Chi.

articles.headline: Ethos Test Reveals Student Body Opinions
articles.body:
According to the results of the recent Ethos Test, 45 per cent of the women and six per cent of the men students tested think that OWU men are inferior to OWU women. Only nine per cent of the men and two per cent of the women think that they are superior.

Another question that was asked was if the attendance ratio should shift to allow more men or more women to enter the University. Eighty-one per cent of the women indicated that they would like to see more males attending OWU. Only one per cent of the women thought that there should be more women on campus.

Lee Doering, chairman of the Ethos Test Subcommittee of the Academic Relations Committee, announced the results of the Ethos survey, which was given in February and March, saying that complete booklets of the graphs compiled from the survey would go on sale in the MUB sometime next week. The price will be 25 cents per person and the booklet will include about 14 of the graphs.

Student-Faculty Drinking
On student-faculty relations, 38 per cent of the students and 18 per cent of the faculty tested thought drinking together would be a good way to improve relations between the two groups. Eighty-three per cent of the students and 50 per cent of the faculty were in favor of more student-faculty discussions.

Social relations is another major area of campus life covered in the survey. There were three questions asked in this area: 1) What are the most important qualities in a man? 2) What are the most imporant qualities in a woman? and 3) What are the most important qualities to you (to the person taking the test), in meeting someone of the opposite sex?

Personality Wanted
The women said they looked for personality, popularity looks, intelligence, money and sex, in that order. Men looked for looks, personality popularity, intelligence, sex and money in a woman. Both wanted personality (80 per cent), intelligence, looks and popularity in a person of the opposite sex they might meet.

"Many different angles should be considered before action can be taken," said Doering when asked what will be done with the information. "They (the results) have illuminated areas of differences between students and faculty by showing what differences exist."

articles.headline: 'Concern' Campaign Deserves Support
articles.body:
The organization at Ohio Wesleyan of the campaign known as "Concern" is welcomed by the Transcript as a positive sign of mature awareness within the student body. This drive for funds could, if successful, make the faculty proposal for scholarships for expelled Southern students a reality, and in this capacity is deserving of our support.

From our editorial vantage point, however, we see in this campaign the greatest challenge to OWU students in many years. The faculty's challenge to the student body has been taken up by a small but dedicated group of students. Their success and effectiveness, however, will only be determined by the support they receive from their fellow students.

That as many students as have, have established this aptly-named organization is indicative of the genesis of a growing and genuine concern on our campus for matters greater in scope than the limits of our ivy-encombered world.

It is, of course, important that we as students take an active part in the formation of University ideals and practices; but it seems to us to be infinitely more important that we concern ourselves with the vital national and international issues of the day, for it is these issues that we must face after our relatively short four-year stay here. If we develop attitudes of complacency now, while we are laying our intellectual foundations for a lifetime, we can have little hope that we shall ever develop, in later years, a constructive interest in vital issues.

The Transcript commends "Concern" with a hope that the student body will support this outstanding project with mature interest and generous financial contributions.

articles.headline: OWU Stands To Gain If Class Plan Succeeds
articles.body:
Students, at least some students, have been vaguely desirable of being treated as academic adults for a long time. They complain of being penalized for class cuts, for being given short range assignments often referred to as busy work, of being fed condensed lecture material that they might understand much better if they could take time out from classes to read and compare articles on the material. In other words, they have objected to what the president of Connecticut Wesleyan refers to as treating "students more as prep-school boys than as adults under guidance."

If the present plan advanced by Prof. Lorish, which will depend mainly on individual study by his students, is realized, then Ohio Wesleyan may well have started to provide an atmosphere for serious long-term study for its students. The proposed program would provide both the academic freedom and the academic responsibility that should be inculcated in young adults.

The Transcript commends this idea and hopes that it will be realized and, being realized, that students will respond sufficiently to warrant continuation and expansion of this type of program at Ohio Wesleyan.

articles.headline: Welcome Extended To Monnett Guests
articles.body:
Monnett Week End is again upon us, and the Ohio Wesleyan community—from senior members of the Board of Trustees to the newest freshmen — will take time out from the routine of bluebooks, MUB time and discussion of campus problems to honor the mothers of Ohio Wesleyan students.

On this week end, an OWU tradition dating to 1900, when the May Queen was a faculty member and the festivities were part of "Violet Day," many of the mothers who visit our campus are returning alumnae, while many will see this school for the first time.

To returning former students, who will find, as they do every year, an Ohio Wesleyan a little different from the one they left but hopefully one capable of maintaining the outstanding record of former years, the Transcript extends a hearty welcome back and its congratulations upon showing a sustained interest in your alma mater in the years since your graduation.

To those to whom OWU and its traditions are new, we also extend a warm welcome to our campus and express a hope that this week end's festivities will mark for you the beginning of a happy association with this institution. In sending your sons and daughters to this university you have expressed your confidence in an institution which many of us love and for which many of us have noble and high ambitions for the future. You and yours can be a part of this future and can help Ohio Wesleyan to achieve the worthy goals and maintain the high standards for which she is known.

And to all mothers, fathers, alumni and friends of Ohio Wesleyan who gather here this week end, the Transcript extends a sincere welcome.

articles.headline: Letters . . .
articles.author: Tom Grissom
articles.body:
Editor, the Transcript:

Today the news stands are flooded with numerous types of publications which all seem to lament the position of America in their alleged race with Russia. Columnists all over the world attempt to stir the freedom - loving citizen to action with varied types of flowery rehetoric. But the apathy of the "freedom-loving citizen" is too great for any single group of writers to extinguish.

Even when a group of well-respected, intelligent and qualified authors present a plan for encouragement of the democratic processes, apathy overwhelms them. At least this is my conclusion when viewing the response that OWU students gave the Freedom House Bookshelf Committee.

More times than not the source of action for worthwhile causes lies in the college campuses of our country. But the typical "don't give a damn" attitude of Wesleyan betrays this belief.

When 2000 students of a school dedicated to "higher Christian ideals" can raise only $372 for the peaceful defeat of communist propaganda, I think there is a definite lack of motivation somewhere in our system.

Eight of the fourteen fraternities on our campus, including my own, couldn't even see fit to give that first penny for the book drive. The amusing part of the whole situation is that Greek groups are supposedly founded on principles of service to others and, above all, of individual freedom. Of course when the fraternity system is attacked by college administrators, these same groups are the first to stand up and blow the horn about the wonderful services they are rendering to the campus and mankind.

The individuals primarily responsible for the collection in the fraternity houses were the Student Forum representatives. Obviously these men were very ineffective in their attempts to solicit funds. Perhaps this is an outgrowth of the fact that the reps are usually just puppets on the strings of the fraternity leaders who are priming them for bigger positions on campus. These men are really not thoroughly satisfied with their positions and thus don't fully carry out the responsibilities that they entail.

For me the book drive served as a mirror with which I could view my self and fellow students with a critical eye. The image I saw was indeed not a pretty one.

I feel our campus is cluttered with a lot of nonfunctional groups and organizations that fail to achieve their established goals and standards. Ohio Wesleyan must surely be

the garden spot for idealism. Now is the time to take stock of ourselves, collectively and individually, and see just where we stand.

Tom Grissom

WSLN Plea

Editor, the Transcript

During this year not much has been heard from the campus radio station, WSLN - FM. We sometimes wonder if we're being heard much on the air either, since we are only an FM operation and the dorm lines have been taken out because of their expense.

The studios have been remodeled, and it is a great improvement. The place no longer looks like a barn with egg cartons on the walls for soundproofing, but now is a pleasant place to work, due to soundboarding on the walls, tile on the floors and the restyling and rewiring of the control room and its equipment.

As an activity, WSLN Radio is dead. As a lab for Radio-TV majors there is enough to do, but here we are again held back by lack of equipment. The facilities for television still lack some of the basic units needed for even closed circuit work.

If perhaps someone in the broadcasting industry could get us over the initial expenses of such a high priced medium, a few ivory tower people would be pleased to discover that telecasting could be a great aid to education, as well as being able to electronically sling commerical trash.

Dave Walker

articles.headline: It Seems To Me...
articles.author: Terry Swango
articles.body:
It seems to me that with the tremendous number of visitors expected this week-end, it will probably become chaotic on campus unless you have some sort of schedule to follow on your OWU fifty-cent tour. Therefore, out of sympathy for my fellow students, I would like to recommend a schedule for travel on Monnett Week End.

Assuming that your parents can get here by early Friday morning, they can go to your 8 o'clock with you. Then if you have an hour at 9 a.m. you can take your parents to watch rehearsals for next year's senior show "William Tell," which will be taking place on the village green (Edwards Field). At 11 you can invite your folks to attend the stimulating and varied study hall and Knitting 112 lab, held in Gray Chapel. (I should, perhaps, remind you to inform your mother and younger sisters not to wear shorts of any description or slacks to the campus.)

Then until 4:15 p.m. there really isn't much to do except take a couple of blue books or something. But at 4:15 you can go and see the academy award-winning production being shown in Phillips Auditorium. With a little luck you haven't seen it more than three or four times anyway.

Don't, however, miss the high points of the evening. These festivities begin quietly, but interestingly, at Austin parking lot at precisely 12:20 a.m. and at 12:25 proceed to the front porch of Austin or Monnett, where you can introduce your parents to your classmates and friends who will, as every night, be quietly sitting and rocking in the chairs on the front porch.

After Saturday morning snap quizzes, the official University schedule will serve as an adequate guide to the day's activities.

Be sure, however, to be in the vicinity of the local taverns at 12:35 a.m., to watch as the fraternity men begin their march on the dorms for their serenades. Notice too, how the tempo and lyrics change as they approach the halls of ivy.

So at last Sunday arrives—but it has been so long and strenuous that after the Convocation and after your parents sadly wave good-bye, you will probably want to see that one area of the campus that you missed on your tour. But a word to the wise should suffice: make your reservations for the infirmary in advance—it will probably be crowded. I've made mine already.

articles.headline: Open Opinions
articles.author: Jerry Sell
articles.body:
Responsibilities Of Convention Aired

Back in 1860 a group of students at Oberlin College got together and decided it would be good fun to have a mock political convention. They got off to a good start, nominating at their first convention that year one A. Lincoln, an Illinois lawyer.

Ever since then, every four years, the Oberlin students have had a good time at their political games. Some strange things have happened, including the 1952 nomination of Senator Wayne Morse for President.

Next week Oberlin will be having their one-hundredth anniversary convention. I'm sure everyone will have a good time. A big party convention is surely a fascinating game, with the deals, smokey rooms, rumors and other traditional accouterments of the political fray.

This summer too a goodly portion of the United States citizenry will spend two weeks in front of their television sets watching the even more exciting real thing. For the TV viewer as well as for the political pilgrim making his personal odyssey to Los Angeles or Chicago there will be two weeks of drama, excitement and thrills, much like the World Series.

I'm sure no one is looking forward to those conventions more than I am. I expect to be fed my meals in front of the television during those crucial weeks. But I'm trying (and it's not an easy task) to look beyond the fun, games and intrigue of the conventions to a more serious evaluation. It's a little frightening to remind yourself that out of all that intrigue, backroom dealing and noisy acclamations will come the choice of the next President of the United States, the man who will have the horrifying task of leading this country and perhaps deciding the fate of the world during the next four years.

The kids at Oberlin can really enjoy their convention. They will have all the thrills and fun of a real political carnival without being faced with the horrible fact that their choice may be the next President. They can afford to get carried away with their big game. Unfortunately, next summer the pros at the real conventions can't let themselves get carried away by their personal fun and games, their personal ambitions and power struggles. The country may get stuck with their choice.

articles.headline: Yellow Paint Saves Mowers
articles.body:
The new additions of yellow paint to various parts of the OWU campus (boulders, rocks, man-hole covers and various other objects which would seem of insignificant importance to the casual observer) is mainly for the protection of machinery which either cuts grass or does other important odd jobs to keep our campus spic and span, according to the Building and Grounds Department.

This explanation is contrary to the general opinion that the new additions were due to a blunder of the requisitioner of supplies, or that a few of the more inclined individuals towards art felt that these new additions would be a credit to the University.

After checking with individuals in the Buildings and Grounds Department and coming up with the same puzzled answers that many students have had concerning the brilliant additions, it was finally determined that "protection must be the answer!"

articles.headline: Prof. Tate Announces Resignation To Take Post At Tulsa Next Fall
articles.body:
Gary L. Tate, assistant professor of English and humanities, recently announced his resignation from the faculty of Ohio Wesleyan University.

He told the Transcript that he is going to the University of Tulsa as an assistant professor.

Prof. Tate obtained his B. A. from Baker University and his M.A. and Ph. D. from the University of New Mexico. He has been a member of the OWU faculty since 1958.

Prof. Tate is the only faculty member from either the English or Humanities Departments to announce his resignation for the coming year.

articles.headline: Greeks To Feed Job Recruiters
articles.body:
Employers conducting interviews on campus next fall will be invited to evening meals at the fraternity houses, according to Peg Boecklin, director of the Placement Office. The plan was initiated by Mrs. Boecklin in a meeting with six fraternity representatives.

All eight of the remaining fraternities have been contacted and have responded favorably to the plan, said Mrs. Boecklin.

Many of the recruiters are looking for summer employees among the undergraduates but never get to meet any of them because of the lack of communication, she said.

Commenting on summer placement for undergraduates, Mrs. Boecklin said, "Our office handled summer placement until about 1955. However, we now do not have enough money to pay an adequate staff to handle this job. We would need three times the personnel we have now to handle the work involved."

articles.headline: Chrysler Art Collection Now In Dayton
articles.author: Ann Wilder
articles.body:
The Chrysler Collection of 121 French masterpieces, valued at about 25 million dollars, is on display at the Dayton Art Institute through May 22.

Many of the giant-sized paintings are suitable only for exhibitions. Monet's "Water Lilies" measures 20 by six and one-half feet, and Delaunay's painting of the Eiffel Tower is 12 feet high.

Director Thomas C. Colt, Jr., quoted in the Dayton Daily News, commented "The paintings represent only a small part of Chrysler's three to four-thousand piece collection, which is one of the largest private collections in the world."

"It is so large," Colt said, "that no museum could think of displaying all of it. Most of the paintings were stored in a large warehouse in New York City, where masterpieces were stacked like storm windows.

"Some of the paintings had been stored in this warehouse for 20 years. Fourteen paintings, by artists such as Gauguin, Picasso, Van Gogh, Derain and Matisse came from the Chrysler apartment," Colt continued.

Pablo Picasso, George Braque, Eugene Vail and Kees Van Dongen are the only artists of the 121 in the collection whose work is still in the process of being completed.

articles.headline: On Campus with Max Shulman
articles.author: Max Shulman
articles.body:
(Author of "I Was a Teen-age Dwarf", "The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis", etc.)

EUROPE MADE SIMPLE: No. 1

Summer vacation is just around the corner, and naturally all of you are going to Europe. Perhaps I can offer a handy tip or two. (I must confess I have never been to Europe myself, but I eat a lot of Scotch broth and French dressing, so I am not entirely without qualification.)

First let me say that no trip to Europe is complete without a visit to England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland, France, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Lichtenstein, Holland, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Russia, Greece, Yugoslavia, Albania, Crete, Sardinia, Sicily, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Lapland, and Andorra.

Let us take up these countries in order. First, England.

The capital of England is London - or Liverpool, as it is sometimes called. There are many interesting things to see in London - chiefly, the changing of the guards. The guards are changed daily. The old ones are thrown away.

Another "must" while in London is a visit to Buckingham Palace. Frequently in the afternoons Her Majesty the Queen comes out on the balcony of the palace and waves to her loyal subjects below. The loyal subjects wave back at the Queen. However, they only continue to wave as long as Her Majesty is waving. This of course is the origin of wave lengths from which we have derived numerous benefits including radio, television and the A&P Gypsies.

Be sure also when you are in London to visit the palace of the Duke of Marlborough. Marlborough is spelled Marlborough, but pronounced Marlboro. English spelling is very quaint but terribly disorganized. The late George Bernard Shaw, author of Jo's Boys, fought all his life to simplify English spelling. He once asked a friend, "What does g-h-o-t-i spell?" The friend pondered a bit and replied, "Goatee." Shaw sniggered. "Pshaw," said Shaw. "G-h-o-t-i does not spell goatee. It spells fish. Gh as in enough, o as in women, ti as in motion."

It must be remembered, however, that Shaw was a vegetarian - which, all in all, was probably a good thing. As Disraeli once remarked to Guy Fawkes, "If Shaw were not a vegetarian, no lamb chop in London would be safe."

But I digress. We were speaking of the palace of the Duke of Marlborough - or Marlboro, as it is called in the United States. It is called Marlboro by every smoker who knows flavor did not go out when filters came in. Be sure you are well supplied with Marlboros when you make your trip abroad. After a long, tiring day of sightseeing, there is nothing so welcome as a fine, flavorful Marlboro and a foot bath with hot Epsom salts.

Epsom salts can be obtained in England at Epsom Downs. Kensington salts can be obtained at Kensington Gardens, Albert salts can be obtained at Albert Hall, Hyde salts can be obtained at Hyde Park, and the crown jewels can be obtained at the Tower of London.

Well sir, now you know all you need to know about England. Next week we will visit the Land of the Midnight Sun - France.

© 1960 Max Shulman

And you also know all you need to know about smoking: Marlboro, if you want the best of the filter cigarettes—Philip Morris Inc.

articles.headline: Newman Club Airs Views On Elections
articles.body:
Can a Roman Catholic be President? He can, members of Ohio Wesleyan's Newman Club concluded, Ellen Cook, sophomore member of the club, told the Transcript last week. This topic was discussed at their Apr. 23 meeting at St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church in Delaware.

There has been, in this presidential election year, much talk over how influential a part religious affiliations will play in the qualifications and appeal of a candidate. Concerning Sen. John Kenedy, the Democratic contender for nomination, the Newman club concluded that his personal philosophy is based on his own beliefs, like anyone else. They feel "he would act on behalf of the majority of the nation."

Miss Cook said that 10 to 15 OWU students of the Roman Catholic faith meet once a month in the Church Rectory, following the 10:30 a.m. mass, for breakfast and an informal discussion session.

Discussion topics at recent meetings have included birth control and religion courses at OWU, Miss Cook said. The purpose of these informal discussions is to answer the many questions which are often asked about the Roman Catholic Church, she added.

Miss Cook said that these meetings were not limited to members of the Catholic Church, and that any students desiring information about the Catholic faith may attend. The next meeting of the Newman Club will be May 15.

articles.headline: OWU Responds To Blood Drive
articles.body:
The response of 142 students to the Delaware County Red Cross blood drive was termed "the usual, amazing support we get from Ohio Wesleyan," by the Rev. Miles Gottschall, William Street Methodist Church minister of music and chairman of the drive.

Out of a total of 205 Delaware blood donors, 69 per cent were Ohio Wesleyan students. "This is a record the Red Cross is truly ready to fully congratulate," said the Rev. Mr. Gottschall. "We can't thank the Wesleyan students enough."

Forty-seven women and 95 men donated 142 pints of blood during the Apr. 22 drive. Beta Theta Pi donated 51 pints of blood to lead the fraternities. Phi Gamma Delta and Alpha Tau Omega were second and third with 14 and 13 donors, respectively.

articles.headline: Debaters Place Second
articles.body:
The OWU Novice Debate team placed second in Ohio State Novice Tournament held at Ashland College, Ashland, O.

The first year debaters, represented on the negative side by John Kercher and Vinny Murphy and on the affirmative by Dave Watt and Chet Cramer, were accompanied on the trip to Ashland by Dick Hattwick, undergraduate fellow in speech, and Robert R. Crosby, associate professor of speech.

The novice debate men won five out of six rounds, with Kercher and Murphy winning all three of their debates, beating Findlay, Ohio University and Wittenberg. Cramer and Watt beat Capital and Western Reserve, losing by a close decision to the Wooster team who went on to win first place in the tournament, Cramer said.

Twenty-two teams from 20 colleges in Ohio went through two rounds of debates in the morning and one round in the afternoon. After the third round an awards assembly was held at which OWU's second place position was announced. Upon hearing of the novice debater's second place win, Hattwick commented that Edward R. Robinson, associate professor of speech, who is the director of debate and forensics, would be pleased to hear that OWU beat Capital, OWU's arch rival in debate. Hattwick also went on to say that the novice debaters have "great potential" for future varsity debate teams.

Cramer remarked that many humorous incidents occurred during the debates. He said that Watt's remark that the opposing team's last comment was unquestionably an "out and out lie," a remark that he supported with sufficient evidence, was a high point in the humor of the day. Later, when his opponents refused to follow his arguments, Watt came through again with the comment that the opposing team "must be deaf." All, including the judge, laughed at this, Cramer said.

articles.body:

In solving the problem, the council of sorority women placed eight items on a list to evaluate local establishments. Among these were the proprietor's enforcement of the Ohio state liquor laws, proper chaperoning for any recognized function and the enforcement of sanitation laws.

Places selected by the committee of students and faculty would be able to entertain students at various registered events, such as parties and dances.

articles.headline: Expelled Student Relates Story Of Southern 'Sit-In' Demonstrations
articles.author: Tom Grissom
articles.body:
(Bernard Lee is a 24 year old Negro who at present is serving as president of the Montgomery Student Protest Committee. Lee makes his home in Norfolk, Va., where he is married and the father of three young children. He was present on our campus this week for meetings and discussions with interested students. This is his story as he related it to Transcript Associate Editor Tom Grissom. — Ed.)

On the morning of Feb. 25, 1960, an organized group of 35 male students from Alabama State College, an all-Negro school at Montgomery, Ala., led by Bernard Lee, filed quietly into the Montgomery County courthouse snack bar and seated themselves, asking to be served.

Because they refused to be served while standing or to take their food outside, the men were denied service of any nature. The group remained silent but never left the snack bar. Soon the proprietor asked the men to leave; but again they failed to leave.

Police Called

Soon the police department was notified, and the chief of the Montgomery Police Department arrived at the courthouse. Again the students ignored persuasion, and remained in their seats.

A short consultation between local officials and the proprietor followed, and it was decided to close the restaurant for the remainder of the day. The group then marched out into an adjacent hallway and stood silently, waiting to see if the snack bar would remain closed.

An hour later the students returned to their campus where a rally of all students followed. Lee and his group were asked at this time to drop the name of the college when participating in these demonstrations. The group then dispersed, failing to acknowledge the plea of the administration.

College Conflict

At this point, said Lee, friction began between the faculty and administration. Many felt the college should be associated with these attempts for racial equality. Others were dead-set against involving the school with political issues. Some professors failed to commit themselves for fear of censorship from administrators.

Alabama Governor John Patterson then dispatched a team of state investigators to inquire into the demonstration and report who was involved. Photos of the sit-in were confiscated and enlarged. These pictures revealed the presence of Lee and eight others, termed "agitators" by Patterson.

After a meeting with the State Board of Education, Patterson sent expulsion papers to the president of Alabama State College on Mar. 4.

Now Youth Minister

Since that day Lee hasn't been allowed to attend any classes at his former school. At present he is employed as the youth minister at the First Baptist Church in Montgomery. This denomination is making possible his tour of college campuses throughout the North.

Lee explained that the group was organized "primarily to identify ourselves with the movement across the South." None in the group felt that the resulting impact would be as great as it was.

On May 9, in the Alabama State Court of Appeals, the nine men who were expelled are to have their case tried. Handling the case will be Negro lawyers Fred Gray, Solomon Seay and Charles Landford. Said Lee, "We only hope by bringing light to the courts of this nation, we may wake up Americans to the unique suppression of individual rights in the South."

articles.headline: Prof. Lorish Plans Experimental Class
articles.body:
An individual study method of teaching his International Politics (317) course is being contemplated by Robert E. Lorish, professor of political science. This would be a small scale test of the type of major programs which have been successful at Connecticut Wesleyan in the last few years, he said.

Lorish said if his hope can be realized he would present a complete syllabus to the students at the first class meeting, including statement of the major program areas of the course, related questions and a bibliography of appropriate books from which the student could choose.

Normally scheduled classes would be replaced with conference hours in which the students might raise questions in the field of interpreting materials covered. When a student felt well enough prepared in terms of the areas and questions on the syllabus he would present himself for, a three to five hour examination prior to the final. The test would include both written and oral work.

Lorish acknowledged that the course would be more than usually difficult because students would still be required to adhere to regular schedule in their other classes, and he felt "that the whole program would require self-discipline on the part of the student."

Lorish said his project was now only "a gleam in my eye" which he hopes to realize through the proper channels, but he stressed the point that the idea is now only tentative.

articles.headline: Debaters Finish Season
articles.body:
The OWU Varsity Debate Team closed out its season last week at the fifth annual Robert S. Marx Tournament at the Sheraton Hotel in Cincinnati, O.

Varsity debaters Charlie Mills and Tony Kidd were eliminated after the sixth round, beating Rochester, St. Louis, and Miami of Ohio and losing to Kentucky (who placed third), Florida, and Miami of Florida (who won the tournament), Edward R. Robinson, associate professor of speech, said.

Prof. Robinson, director of debate, said the 28 schools represented at the invitational tournament were some of the top teams in the country, and it was quite an honor for Ohio Wesleyan to have been invited this year. He said OWU was one of two Ohio teams to be invited, the other being Miami of Ohio. The last time Ohio Wesleyan was invited to attend was in 1956.

Dr. Robinson added that he will mail out next year's national debate topic to interested future debaters as soon as it comes in, if they will leave their name with him or in the office of the secretary of the Speech Department.

articles.headline: Burns Lists Four Faculty Appointments For Chemistry, Economics, Languages
articles.body:
The Appointment of four new faculty members was announced last week by George W. Burns, vice-president and dean of the University. The four are Lawrence B. Wick, associate professor of chemistry; Subbiah Kannappan, assistant professor of economics; William V. Glebe, assistant professor of German, and Fernando Carrera, instructor in Spanish.

Prof. Wick, who is 43, obtained his A.S. from Jackson Junior College, and his B.S., M.S. and Ph. D. from the University of Michigan. He has been employed as a research chemist for the Tennessee Eastman Corp., in Oak Ridge, Tenn., and as a research laboratory associate in organic and radioisotopes for the Glidden Company of Chicago, Ill.

His teaching experience includes four years as an assistant professor at Northern Illinois State College and one year at Kansas State College. He is now finishing his second year at Drury College where he is an associate professor of chemistry.

Now At Reed

Prof. Subbiah Kannappan is 32 years of age and is now employed at Reed College as an assistant professor of economics. Prof. Kannappan obtained an M.A. from Madras University in India and an M.A. and Ph. D. from the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy. He also did post-doctoral study at the University of Chicago.

He was an editoral assistant for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, a research assistant for the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the director of research in labor and industrial relations at Xavier Institute of Labor, Jamshedpur, India, an economist and member of the Urban Planning Team for the Ford Foundation, New Delhi, India, and a consulting economist of the National Planning Association.

Prof. Kannappan spent one year as an assistant professor of economics at Madras University, one year as a teaching assistant at Tufts University and is now finishing his first year at Reed College.

Studied In Canada

Prof. Glebe, who is 39, obtained his B.A. from the University of Toronto, his M.A. from the University of Alberta, and his Ph. D. from the University of Washington.

He taught as an instructor in German at Concordia Collegiate Institute Preparatory School for two years before going to the University of Washington as a part-time instructor in German. Prof. Glebe has been at Lehigh University since 1956, where he is now an assistant professor of German.

Prof. Carrera received his B.A. from the University of Mexico and his M.A. from the University of Oregon. He is now working on his Ph. D.

Prof. Carrera, who is 28, has taught as an assistant in Spanish at the University of Oregon, instructor in Spanish at the University of Mexico and has been an instructor at Wabash College since last fall.

articles.headline: OWU Faculty Pay Scales Improved
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan University advanced to a "C" rating this year, in terms of faculty pay scales, two members of the American Association of University Professors explained last week.

President Robert H. Ross, associate professor of English and humanities, and President-elect Robert M. Montgomery, professor of religion, praised OWU's pay-status on two counts:

1) The administration's willingness to participate in the voluntary AAUP rating program and

2) The fact that OWU was one of the three Ohio liberal arts colleges that earned C's in two categories (Oberlin and Kenyon were the other two).

Participating colleges are rated on a scale from A to F in two categories — minimum pay levels for the four teaching ranks and average faculty member's pay.

Ohio Wesleyan's D rating last year was about average for reporting colleges, Profs. Ross and Montgomery explained, and this year's C grades are above average. They also said that no reporting college in Ohio received above a C in either category.

The two professors stressed that a college's academic rating depends on the qaulity of its faculty, and good faculty members can be attracted and retained only with a better than average scale of compensation.

They went on to say that because of the increasing need for people with doctor's degrees, graduate schools will get stiffer than ever in the next decade. Thus only applicants from highly regarded undergraduate schools will be favorably considered for admission.

articles.headline: W. R. Bennett Resigns Alum Office Post
articles.body:
William R. Bennett, who has been the assistant director of Alumni Affairs for the past two years, recently announced his resignation.

Bennett is an OWU graduate of the class of 1958 and has held his present post since the fall of that year.

He has resigned in order to continue his education at the University of Connecticut, in Stores, Conn. He will enter a program to obtain his doctorate in the field of international relations, he told the Transcript last week.

He described his job here as "one of the most rewarding experiences that I've ever had."

Howard E. Strauch, director of alumni affairs, had this to say about Bennett's resignation, "Mr. Bennett has done an excellent job for us at OWU in general alumni activity, promotion of the alumni fund and in the area of admission, and we are pleased that his experiences here have encouraged him to remain in the field of higher education. In order to filfull his goals, it is, of course, necessary for him to go on for an advanced degree."

articles.headline: Grade Survey Results Told
articles.body:
The results of a survey on the "Plus and Minus Grading System," taken by the Academic Relations Committee, were revealed last week by Matt Finkin, committee sub-chairman in charge of the survey.

The purpose of the survey was to determine whether a revision of the grading system to allow for pluses and minuses would be advisable.

After investigating a representative sampling of student grades (i.e., one out of four anonymous seniors provided by Registrar Allan C. Ingraham's office) the committee reported that the cumulative point averages of only two per cent of the sampling would increase, whereas the other 98 per cent would decrease in varying degrees.

Although there were several students with 30 to 40 hours of plus, the Committee regarded them in the light of a far greater number of students who had corresponding hours of minus.

Finkin informed the Transcript that the Committee will not suggest a point revision of the grading system, since an overwhelming majority of the student body would not benefit from such a revision.

articles.headline: 'Golden Demon' Proves To Be Rare Experience
articles.author: Connie McNeil
articles.body:
"The Golden Demon" is a rare experience for the movie-goer; it is a work of art. The photography accomplishes the feat of making nearly every camera view memorable, not in the American colossal manner, but in the exquisite Japanese style.

A careful blend of sombre blacks, rich reds and delicate pastels expressed the mood of the movie. The flight of birds silhouetted against a blazing dawn and a morbidly powerful fire scene were especially impressive. However, several, scenes were too dark and obscured the action for prolonged periods.

The acting cannot be fully appraised from the visual viewpoint only, but at this disadvantage, I still was moved by the refined, but expressive faces of the leads. The music contributed to the bizarre mood as fully as the photography.

The story, itself, dwells on character destruction through greed. The plot moves tragically toward the ending, which destroys the total effect with its audience-aimed happy ending. Although I am aware of the resurrecting power of forgiveness which the ending implies, I found the treatment inconsistent and melodramatic.

In spite of the above criticism, I consider this movie one which American producers might well imitate. Once the screen industry approaches movies as works of art and begins directing photography, music and sensitive acting toward a higher goal than their present commercialism, it might create more than just marketable products.

("The Golden Demon" was the last offering of the 1959-60 Movie-Lecture series.—Ed.)

articles.headline: OWU-GIS Program Continues To Grow
articles.body:
The Ohio Wesleyan Red Cross-GIS program has tripled in the last three years, averaging about 150 students each week, according to Mickey Foster, GIS chairman. Foster attributed OWU's increased interest to efforts of fraternity and sorority representatives.

Providing a resocializing experience for teenagers at Girls Industrial School and a learning experience for OWU students, the program has included pizza parties, swimming parties, dessert parties at fraternity houses and rock'n'roll sessions at the GIS cottages with student combos.

An Ohio Wesleyan-GIS talent show last month at Sanborn Hall, a dance at Rathbone Ranch sponsored by the Red Cross and ROTC Chaplain's Corps with the Sigma Chi and Kappa Sigma pledge classes have rounded out the season.

GIS girls have come to campus for a performance of the "Messiah" and a dress rehearsal of "South Pacific."

Praising the program on behalf of the GIS staff, Miss Colleen O'Dell, director of recreation, commented, "Through the program, the girls gain an insight into activities they've never had the opportunity to see before.

"We can teach synchronized swimming, but it's seeing a Dolphin show that shows the girls what it can be and gives them the incentive to do it themselves."

Trips to Ohio Wesleyan have given them an opportunity to get an "over-all picture of college life," she said.

Ohio Wesleyan student interest in the girls and their problems is "one of the great helps to the answer of juvenile delinquency," according to Miss Abbie Semans, head of the Delaware Red Cross chapter.

Prior to planning OWU-GIS activities each semester, GIS superintendent M. B. McLain and Dr. Mary Price, chief psychologist, explained the program's policies and goals to fraternity presidents, sorority representatives and about 70 OWU students. Johnny Rowland, owner of Holiday Hill, also taught recreational skills for use at GIS.

Suggesting ways of improvement, Miss O'Dell stated that the program would be more effective with a "more stable number of students." Participation has declined this spring, presumably because of conflicting campus activities and bad weather. Foster expects increased interest next fall.

Planned by six student supervisors and fraternity and sorority representatives, the program operates in conjunction with the Delaware Red Cross chapter. Co-chairmen are Foster and Sue Wilkinson.

articles.headline: Change Not To Affect Methodist Policies
articles.body:
The abolishment of the central jurisdiction of the Methodist Church would probably have little immediate effect on segregation policies of Methodist Church throughout the South, according to Russell Bayliff, professor of sociology, and former pastor of William Street Methodist Church. The Southern lawmaker is known for his ability to invent ways of getting around the law," Prof, Bayliff said. "There is little doubt in my mind," he said, "that if the central jurisdiction is abolished, many Church leaders on the local level will follow the example of the several Southern states which have enacted Massive Resistance laws in their effort to avoid integration in the public schools."

Prof. Bayliff said that there are many ways in which the Southern church leaders might try to conform to the action of the General Conference, and yet ignore the very spirit of it, if the central jurisdiction is abolished.

Hopes of this taking place look very dim however, for a compromise plan which would retain the central jurisdiction seems to be getting considerable support at the current session of the Methodist General Conference at Denver, Colo.

Under the present structure, the Methodist Church is organized for administrative purposes into five regional jurisdictions of predominantly white membership and a nation-wide central jurisdiction to which 97 per cent of the Negro churches belong," Prof. Bayliff said.

According to Prof. Bayliff, the central jurisdiction is the result of a compromise which was worked out by the Northern and Southern branches of Methodism which reunited in 1939, after a century of separation. He said that the abolishment of the central jurisdiction would mean placing Negro and white churches into the same annual conferences.

This would mean that Negro and White leaders of the churches would be brought together to transact their business during the annual conference session. This would create a problem of housing as well as of dining facilities," Prof, Bayliff said.

Knowing the present attitude of many Southern church leaders, it is quite likely that they might resort to having separate business sessions should they be forced into the same annual conference, the Negroes having their meeting in the morning and the whites having theirs in the afternoon," Prof. Bayliff said.

"The possibility of this coming about in the very near future is highly improbable, however," Prof. Bayliff declared. "What is more likely to happen," he said, "is that Southern lawmakers will devise some scheme to keep this from taking place."

Alabama and Mississippi have taken such action, passing state laws which would permit local churches to withdraw from their parent denominations and take possession of local church buildings.

While no mention of the Methodist Church or segregation is contained in any of these laws, they seem to have been passed with both clearly in mind, Prof. Bayliff indicated. They provide generally that a congregation may withdraw from its parent denomination and claim title to the Church building if a two-thirds vote of its adult membership is secured.

articles.headline: Quartet Outstanding
articles.author: Linda Merkle
articles.body:
To a sparse but appreciative audience at Sanborn Hall last week, the Alard String Quartet gave a moving concert.

"Quartet in G Minor, Op. 10" by Debussy was exceptionally noteworthy as a brilliantly preformed number. The "Assez vif et bien rythem" movement from the work, with its exciting rhythm and interesting chord progressions, was the highpoint of the evening.

"Quartet in C Major (Dissonant), K. 465," by Mozart was dynamically and superbly done.

The quartet, in residence at Wilmington College, is made up of Donald Hopkins, Joanne Zagst, Raymond Page and Leonard Feldman. The group has performed widely in the Midwest and Southwest and has appeared at Town Hall in New York City. The quartet won the National Federation of Music Clubs' Young Artist's Award in 1955.

Their concert last Tuesday was one of a series of appearances at several colleges and universities throughout the Midwest.

articles.headline: Vote To Decide On Highway Site
articles.body:
The future of the long-discussed expressway to by-pass the Delaware business district will be decided by Delaware voters in the fall election, when a bond issue for the road will be on the ballot, according to Don Mackley, Delaware city manager.

If the bond issue passes, it will still be four or five years before the highway is completed. If vetoed, the plans will be cancelled, the city manager declared.

The state highway department is holding a public hearing June 2 to discuss the proposed super-highway, according to Russell Bayliff, professor of sociology and Delaware city clerk. Such a hearing is required by law when relocation of a state highway is involved.

articles.headline: OWU Men Head State Circle K
articles.body:
For the second consecutive year Ohio Wesleyan Circle K men have been elected to the two top positions in the Ohio District Circle K organization.

Junior Bob Maxwell of Delaware and Tom Grissom, a sophomore from Louisville, Ky., were elected governor and secretary, respectively, for the state in 1960-61.

Maxwell steps up to the governorship from his present post as district secretary. The retiring governor is Bob Newcomb, an OWU senior from Harlan, Ky.

Elections were held at the third annual Circle K Convention held at Capital University last week.

articles.headline: Committee Prepares For Campus Future
articles.body:
In an attempt to prepare for the problems expected to be faced by the University in the 1960's and 70's, the Faculty-Administration Committee of Nine has been taking "a good-hard look at the objectives and goals of the University and the way we are achieving them," George W. Burns, vice-president and dean of the University, reported.

"From deliberations there may come recommendations for doing our educational jobs in a better way," he continued.

In operation for three months, the committee has drawn up for its own guidance "a hypothetical statement of University principles and aims," according to committee member Loyd D. Easton, professor of philosophy. "This was not prepared for release," he stated, "but only for the committee's own consideration."

Members Appointed
Administrative members of the committee, appointed by President David A. Lockmiller, include Dean Burns; D. J. Hornberger, vice-president and treasurer; W. Noel Johnston, vice-president of University relations, and Robert Meyer, controller.

Three of the faculty members on the committee were selected earlier by President Lockmiller and Vice-President Burns to attend the Danforth Foundation Workshop at Boulder, Colo., this summer along with Dean Burns. They are William A. Bultmann, associate professor of history; Robert H. Ross, associate professor of English, and Robert L. Wilson, professor of mathematics.

Two other faculty members, Prof. Easton and Ronald R. Green, professor of psychology, were elected at the January faculty meeting.

Fundamental Matters
In looking ahead, Dean Burns predicted that the committee would be operating "at least through next year, as we're dealing with matters too fundamental to be hurried. The information received at the Danforth Workshop will be coordinated with the work of the committee," he added.

The closest thing to a committee of this sort previously in operation on the Ohio Wesleyan campus was the Staff Papers Committee of former President Arthur S. Flemming. It had the same general goals, according to Dean Burns, but it was attempting to make problems concrete and to raise questions.

"We are looking for solutions," Burns stated. "We are seeking any information bearing upon the University's ability to do a better job."

articles.headline: Pre-Medical Exams Held Monnett Day
articles.body:
Monnett Day will not be a holiday for junior pre-med majors. The Medical College Admission Test, required for admission by member colleges of the Association of American Medical Colleges, will be given here on May 7 to students who plan to enter medical school in the fall of 1961, according to Chester O. Mathews, director of the educational research and evaluation service.

Since the test is administered on a nationwide basis and must be given simultaneously in all parts of the country, OWU applicants must take the test on the campus holiday, Mathews explained.

The test takes six hours for completion and consists of a general scholastic ability test, a test of the candidate's understanding of modern society and an achievement test in science.

Medical schools requiring the test use it to supplement other information about the applicant, Mathews added.

articles.headline: Olympic Prospects Here For Monnett Track Meet
articles.author: Stu Rose
articles.body:
Saturday will be no holiday for the OWU trackmen, when they face a University of Kentucky powerhouse at Selby Field.

Three Olympic prospects and an ex-Ohio state champ will lead the Wildcat squad in the Monnett Week End clash at 1:30 p. m.

Kentucky Coach Don Seaton, a former Olympic hurdler himself, is grooming half-miler E. G. Plummer, miler and twomiler Press Whelan and 440-man Roger Gum for berths on the U.S. team.

Records In Danger

Both Plummer and Whelan are expected to set Selby Field records in their events, unless Coach Seaton enters them in other races to garner additional points.

Dave Franta of Mansfield, O., state pole valut champion in high school, is the Wildcats jack-of-all-trades. Franta, besides pole-vaulting, broad jumps 23 feet and runs the 220 low hurdles and the sprints.

Bishop Coach Sterling Geesman predicted that his charges would make a good showing against the star-studded Kentucky squad.

Sprinter John Guy, who was expected to lead the Bishops in Saturday's meet, may not run because of a pulled leg muscle sustained in the Capital meet.

Quadrangular Here Tuesday

articles.headline: Baseballers Face Otters In Monnett Day Feature
articles.body:
Last Friday the OWU baseball team defeated Denison 9-5 at Granville. The Bishops will be out to improve their 5-2 record Saturday as Otterbein comes to Edwards Field in the big Monnett Day game.

OWU and Otterbein have met once already this season with the Bishops coming out on top 7-0 in their finest game thus far. Southpaw Toby Aaron pitched, earning Athlete of the Week honors for his contributions. Aaron again will be the probable starting pitcher for the Red and Black Saturday. He will have to be very effective in order to stop the slugging of Jack Pietila, Otterbein's leading hitter. His recent hitting has boosted his average to .417, third best in the Ohio Conference.

Otters Good Hitters

Otterbein's present record stands at 2-3, with losses to OWU, Ohio Northern and Heidelberg and victories over Muskingum and Kenyon. Outside of the OWU game, the Otters have proven themselves to be a good hitting team. They have scored 29 runs in the five games for a 5.8 average.

Last season, Otterbein finished with a 3-8 Ohio Conference record which placed them one slot below the Bishops in the final standings.

Bob Olson, the Bishop's center-fielder, will match his hitting talents against those of Pietila of Otterbein. Olson was the leading hitter in the Ohio Conference last week a lofty .538 average. Olson also was leading the Ohio Conference in three other departments. His 14 hits, 12 runs, and 5 stolen bases were all tops.

Leading Hitters

Catcher John MacIlwaine and shortstop Hal Hendershot are the other Bishops among the conference's leading hitters, both sporting nifty .391 averages. MacIlwaine also leads the conference with 11 RBI's and 2 home runs.

Against Denison last Friday OWU came up with three runs in the first and ninth innings to win 9-5. Toby Aaron went all the way on the mound while posting his second victory of the season. Aaron gave up five runs on 11 scattered hits. He struck out four and walked five.

Gerosa Leads Attack

Don Gerosa belted two doubles and a home run to lead the Bishop hitting attack. His home run was a tremendous blast in the ninth inning that accounted for three runs.

articles.headline: Russians Lose To OWU In Female Superiority
articles.author: John Linton and Rog Lockwood
articles.body:
This time the Russians have gone too far! They may be ahead of us in the missile race, their leadership may be more democratic than Ohio Wesleyan's and they may win the next war, but we refuse to tolerate their outrageous claims that their women are superior to ours.

Let us make a brief analytical study of the two systems — the one of the Russians and the other of Ohio Wesleyan's women — to affirm our contention.

N. Romanov, chairman of the Organizational Bureau of the Union of Sport Societies and Organizations of the USSR (OBUSPOUSSR) had this to say about the Russian physical fitness program for women:

'At present, several million people already take setting up exercises at work. Also, athletic grounds will be set up at factory yards, industrial settlements, parks, hotels, apartment houses, collective farms and educational establishments.'

The OWU Coed

But we can dismiss this impressive list with a mere wave of the hand, for who does more walking than the Ohio Wesleyan woman? And what coed on this campus does not do a sitting up exercise at seven in the morning as she wakes from peaceful slumber?

Furthermore, we point with pride to the agility and quick manuverability our girls display on the porches of the several dorms when the 10:30, 12:30 and 1:30 sparring bouts take place.

But let us examine the more practical aspects of the local program. Weeks of ardous training on the Edwards Field archery range, under the expert tutelage of Robin Hood Geesman, make fine bowmen of our women.

Liberal Minded

Not only does the Russian women claim to be physically stronger, she also claims to be better dressed. Preposterous! Only last week, the Association of Women Students (AWS) decreed it would consider letting our women use their own discretion in dressing themselves. Although we must admit that the old AWS policy of edict and decree was on a par with the Russians, this new departure shows a liberal attitude that threatens to leave the Russians far behind.

One thing the US and USSR do seem to agree on is that the woman's place is not in the home. Russian women are active in producing weapons for defense, weapons for offense and Russian children. Not to be outdone, Ohio Wesleyan women are active in sorority meetings, corridor meetings, committee meetings, and meetings of Big Board, Little Board, In Board and Out Board.

All these things considered, the reader still might question the comparative domestic program of ours to the war-geared athletic program of Russian women. After much reflection on the matter we concede the point that Russia may well win World War Three. But, lest we forget, the Fourth World War will be fought with bows and arrows, and to us that victory must come.

articles.headline: Five Varsity Contests Slated For Monnett Day
articles.author: Bob Moyers
articles.body:
Other Sports Also Readied

With five varsity teams in action along with a host of other sporting events, the Ohio Wesleyan sport fan should be well-rewarded with this spring's Monnett Day sports schedule.

The week end sports spectacular will feature the varsity sports of lacrosse, baseball, tennis, golf and track plus several minor activities in the sporting vein.

Saturday will be the big day for the sports enthusiast with a complete slate of sporting events scheduled.

The opening attraction for the day will be an exhibition of gymnastics and modern dance in military fashion by the Air Force ROTC. Beginning at 9 a.m. the men in blue will favor the Monnett visitors with a full dress parade on the Selby Stadium battlefield.

OSU Out For Revenge

After the military has faded into their cloud of dust, the OWU lacrosse team will enter the Selby arena to face the revenge-minded Ohio State lacrosse squad.

Earlier this season the OWU stickmen dusted off the Buckeyes, 13-8, but Coach Fred Myers is looking forward to an interesting rematch and expects OSU "to be up" for the game.

The morning's other sporting event will match Dick Gordon's fine golf team against Heidelberg at the Delaware Country Club. The talented Bishops will be favored to repeat over the Student Princes. In an earlier match, the OWU linkmen swamped Heidelberg by a 15 1/2 to 4 1/2 score.

Following the morning's activities, the spectator can enter into the actual competition of weightlifting and calorie-counting, depending on what or how much food he consumes at the training tables in the respective dorms and local eating establishments.

Trackmen Face Wildcats

At 1:30 p.m. the spotlight will be focused upon Selby Stadium where the OWU cindermen will tangle with the Wildcats of the University of Kentucky in one of the day's top features. The Southeastern Conference power will present a star-studded team against the Bishops, featuring three promising Olympic prospects. Although the OWU trackmen will be decided underdogs, Coach Sterling Geesman should have his athletes in top form in an attempt to put a hurdle across the path of the rampaging Wildcats.

Directly to the south of the stadium, the Bishop tennis team will continue its battle for top seeded position in the upcoming OC tourney in a match with Kenyon at 2 p.m. Based on last week's results, the netters were unbeaten in the conference with an impressive 7-0 record.

Olson Leads Conference

At the same time, Les Michael's unusual baseball team will face Otterbein at Edwards Field. The batmen's roster includes Bob Olson, the conference's leading hitter, and long ball hitter Harvey Ford, who is one of the league leaders in strikeouts at the plate. Pitcher Dave Johnston is unbeaten in conference play, but he also has the distinction of leading the league in bases on balls.

Other different athletic events will also be going on throughout the afternoon. In the cross country feature of the day, Ted Gathany, OWU sports publicist, will run against himself when he tries to be at every event at the same time.

Also at Gray Chapel, 50 pert and pretty OWU fillies will prance into the winners circle at the Monnett style show.

Greatest Splash On Earth

The evening's sporting entertainment will be provided by the Dolphin Club in a water show entitled "The Greatest Splash on Earth." Based on a circus theme, the show will be presented at 7:45 and 9:15 p.m. on Saturday. The show will also be given on Thursday and Friday nights.

As the evening progresses, the annonymous OWU rifle club, composed of anyone who wants to join, will attract attention at many of the local drinking establishments. Prizes will be given to the person who can take the most shots before dropping out of the competition.

As a climax to the day's activities, spectators are cordially invited to watch some of the latest holds and improvisions of the art of wrestling to be held at several outdoor arenas located conviently in front of Austin, Monnett and Stuyvesant Halls.

articles.headline: Kenyon Nips Lacrossers In Overtime
articles.body:
In a hard fought contest in which the lead changed hands seven times, the Ohio Wesleyan lacrosse team lost a heartbreaker last Friday afternoon to the Lords of Kenyon, 11-10 in a double overtime.

Kenyon started the scoring in the first quarter and at the end of the quarter they led 3-2. In the second quarter the Bishops came back and outscored the Lords four goals to two and led at halftime 6-5.

Both teams scored once in the third quarter and in the fourth quarter Kenyon found the nets for three goals while the Bishops could only pick up two goals. The score at the end of regulation time was all tied up, 9-9.

In the first overtime both teams were held scoreless. Kenyon scored first in the second overtime while Jack Orin was serving a penalty and the Lords led 10-9. Kenyon scored again and led 11-9. Ohio Wesleyan came back with the last goal of the game on a shot by Max Urick that made the final score 11-10.

Bishop Scoring

The Bishop stickmen where led by Bill Keating, Jeff Fox and Urick who picked up two goals each. Bill Bishop and Tom "Flash" Howell each picked up a goal and one assist. Rog Auker and Dick Heaston each had one goal and Chuck Jantz had an assist.

Rog Auker, one of the Bishops top scorers, was hurt in the first quarter and had to be taken out for the rest of the game. Keating took over for Auker and scored both of his goals in the second quarter.

Kenyon was led by Hobler who scored four goals and by Farr who picked up five assists.

Coach Fred Myers felt his defensive men were not up to par against Kenyon. Myers said that the defense will have to work harder on checking their men closer and keeping the score down.

Face Denison Today

Today the Ohio Wesleyan stickmen meet Denison at Granville. Denison has only lost one game this year, that being to Oberlin. Myers believes this is going to be another "real rough game."

The big Monnett Week End lacrosse game will be this Saturday morning at Selby Stadium when the Bishops will face Ohio State for the second time this year.

articles.body:
Don Gerosa, sophomore from Mahopac, N. Y., has been selected Athlete of the Week for his power hitting and fine all-round play in the Denison baseball game last week.

After a dismal early season start, Gerosa has almost sewed up a starting berth in the OWU outfield with his performance in the Denison game.

Gerosa was the mainstay in the Bishop attack against Denison with two doubles and a home run and drove in four runs in OWU's 9-5 victory.

His two doubles tied an OWU record, and his homer came with two men on the top of the ninth to ice the game. Coach Les Michael noted the home run was the longest that he has seen for the past two seasons.

articles.headline: Sailors Will Berth In Finals
articles.author: Dave Sloan
articles.body:
The Ohio Wesleyan sailors squeezed into the Midwest Champs Regatta by edging Xavier for the third qualifying position in the last week's qualifying regatta at the Leatherlips Yacht Club. Next week end the Bishops travel to the Detroit Yacht Club Regatta for stiff competition against new and old competitors.

At Detroit, OWU will be sailing against Wooster, Xavier, Michigan State and Wayne State who were defeated by the bishops in previous regattas. Notre Dame and the University of Detroit are about even with the OWU team, the standings being one and one between the two schools.

However, Big Ten schools, such as Ohio State and the University of Michigan will give Ohio Wesleyan real competition.

The weather did not help the Bishop hosts last week end, as a rainy Saturday made uncomfortable sailing. The weather did not dampen the Ohio State team, however, as they sailed out on top with 50 points, followed closely by Wooster College with 47 points.

The Bishops, however, were more concerned with their own position, for they needed the third place to qualify. At the end of the regatta, OWU shared the number three slot with Xavier, both with 36 1/2 points.

The determining factor in breaking the tie in favor of Ohio Wesleyan was that the Bishops bettered Xavier in the majority of the individual races in the regatta.

Linda Esslinger skippered in the A division for the Bishops and with George Robinson and Thom Dunn as crewmen, collected 15 1/2 out of the possible 30 points.
